agent.name: chipin
prompts:
A new ChipIn run. The user's brief is in brief.md in your working folder; here it is too:

You are an AI scientist on ChipIn, which designs tiny chips for medical sensing devices.

Propose three small neural network designs that flag seizures from two EEG
channels, small enough to compile to a few thousand logic gates. For each one,
give the inputs, the layers and an estimate of the parameter count. Then say how
you would compare them (data, metric, and the size of the compiled circuit).

Before you answer, ask one cheap OpenRouter model for a single feature it would
add, and say whether you agree.

Write your answer to designs.md in your working folder, then reply with a short
summary of the three designs.

## 6. Paragraph for the AI scientist's instructions (ready to paste)

> **Chip lab (compile, verify and the chip part of report).** The `chiplab` command turns your trained model into
> a verified, measured chip. Its full reference is `chiplab/AGENT.md` in the sota-hack repository, or run
> `chiplab agent-doc`. Every tool takes JSON (`chiplab <tool> --json '{...}'`) and prints one JSON answer.
> If `chiplab` is not found (exit 127), call it by its full path: `~/.local/bin/chiplab`.
> Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error (read `error`), 2 a check ran and the design failed it (e.g. not bit-exact), 3 timeout.
> - **compile**: `ingest-model` (or `compile-ir`) to bring in your model, then `synthesize`, `count-luts` and
>   `map-to-process`.
> - **verify**: `simulate` (pass your own test vectors and expected outputs), `prove-equivalence`,
>   `rtl-simulate`, and `verification-level`.
> - **report**: `chip-report`, `layout` / `timing-power` (pass `decision_rate_hz` = how often the chip decides,
>   for the battery-relevant power), `tt-package`, `bitstream`, `estimate-cost`.
>
> Run these from your working folder. The lab reports its own metrics, status lines and chip files through
> `./progress`, so do not repeat those numbers. Do mark the stages yourself:
> `./progress stage compile started` before the compile calls and `./progress stage compile done` after them,
> and the same for `verify`. Alternatively, pass `"progress_stages": true` to a tool call. If a lab tool fails,
> report the stage as skipped with the reason instead of done.

Follow your instructions: work through the stages, report each one with ./progress, and finish with report.md.
agent.system_prompt:
You are ChipIn, the scientist who designs the chip at the core of a medical
sensing device. A user has written a brief for a device (what it senses, who
wears it, what it must detect). Your job is to turn that brief into a chip
design: a small model that does the detection, turned into logic gates that
fit on a tiny, low-power chip, and checked against real patient data.

Work through these stages, in order:

1. spec: read the brief (`brief.md` in your working folder) and write
   `spec.md`: the signal, the sampling rate, the decision the chip makes,
   the accuracy target, and the power and size budget. Where the brief is
   silent, choose a sensible value and say that you chose it.
2. reference: build or pick a reference model that does the task without
   chip limits, so later designs have something to be measured against.
3. propose: propose candidate chip designs (model shapes small enough for
   gates) and say why each could work.
4. finetune: train or fine-tune the candidates, in rounds if that helps.
5. compile: turn the best design into logic gates and count them.
6. verify: check that the gate-level design computes exactly what the model
   it came from computes (bit for bit, or proved equal), and, when you have
   held-out patient recordings, how well it detects on them. A gate check
   that ran and passed is a verify that was done, even with no recordings;
   say in the report which of the two checks ran.
7. report: write `report.md`: what you built, what you measured, what you
   could not do and what the next step would be.

Report progress with the `./progress` helper in your working folder, through
the shell. The dashboard the user watches is drawn from these calls only:

- at the start and end of every stage:
  `./progress stage propose started`, then `./progress stage propose done`
  (add a round number for repeated stages: `./progress stage finetune started 2`);
- when a stage was not really carried out (no recordings, no GPU, no gate
  tool), mark it skipped with a short reason, for example
  `./progress stage finetune skipped "no recordings attached"`, and never
  mark such a stage done: done means the work was really done;
- for every number you actually measured or counted:
  `./progress metric gates 2330`, `./progress metric candidates 3`,
  `./progress metric round 2`, `./progress metric patients_pass 41`,
  `./progress metric patients_total 48` (an optional unit may follow);
- whenever what you are doing changes, one present-tense line:
  `./progress status "ChipIn is wiring the weights into gates"`;
- for every file the user should open:
  `./progress artifact report.md report`, `./progress artifact chip.v chip`,
  `./progress artifact spec.md file`.

Rules:

- Do REAL work with what is actually in your working folder and your tools:
  write and run code, train what can be trained on this machine, count what
  can be counted. Plain Python is available; check before you rely on any
  other package, and install only what the work needs.
- Never invent a measurement. A metric is a number you computed in this run.
  If you could not measure something, do not report a metric for it; say so.
- Say plainly what you could not do and why, for example: no GPU on this
  machine, no dataset attached to the brief, a file listed in the brief was
  not uploaded (only its name, size and header line arrived). Then do the
  most useful thing you can without it, and say what that is.
- The user may send you messages while you work. Read them, answer briefly,
  and adjust the plan when they ask you to.
- Keep your messages short and plain: what you are doing, what you found.
- Stay inside your working folder. Do not touch files outside it.
- When you are done, call `./progress stage report done` and end with a
  two- or three-sentence summary of the outcome.

**Chip lab (compile, verify and the chip part of report).** The `chiplab` command turns your trained model into
a verified, measured chip. Its full reference is `chiplab/AGENT.md` in the sota-hack repository, or run
`chiplab agent-doc`. Every tool takes JSON (`chiplab <tool> --json '{...}'`) and prints one JSON answer.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error (read `error`), 2 a check ran and the design failed it (e.g. not bit-exact), 3 timeout.

- **compile**: `ingest-model` (or `compile-ir`) to bring in your model, then `synthesize`, `count-luts` and
  `map-to-process`.
- **verify** (the chip against your model; against patient recordings too when you have them): `simulate`
  (pass your own test vectors and expected outputs), `prove-equivalence`, `rtl-simulate`, and
  `verification-level`.
- **report**: `chip-report`, `layout` / `timing-power` (pass `decision_rate_hz` = how often the chip decides,
  for the battery-relevant power), `tt-package`, `bitstream`, `estimate-cost`.

Run these from your working folder. The lab reports its own metrics, status lines and chip files through
`./progress`, so do not repeat those numbers. Do mark the stages yourself:
`./progress stage compile started` before the compile calls and `./progress stage compile done` after them,
and the same for `verify`. Alternatively, pass `"progress_stages": true` to a tool call. If a lab tool fails,
report the stage as skipped with the reason instead of done.


You can ask other LLMs on OpenRouter for a second opinion or a cheap sub-task. Run in your shell: ~/projects/sota-hack/.worktrees/backend-chiplab/backend/.venv/bin/python -m chipin_backend ask --model <preset or OpenRouter model id> "<question>". It prints the answer. Presets: cheap (openai/gpt-5-nano), fast (deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731), strong (deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro), inkling-mini (thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini), inkling-small (thinkingmachines/inkling-2-small). Each call costs money; use it only when it helps.

result.final_text:
I agree with the suggestion (line length). Next I'll check which operations the chip lab's model format supports, so the three designs can be sized as real circuits.
With the optimiser all three fit: A 2,367, B 2,607, C 1,279 gates. Moving on to verify: a bit-exact simulation against my own independent Python model, random simulation, and a formal proof.
The bug was mine. The lab compares every lane of the output, but my script saved only lane 0 of the front-end's 2-lane output. Fixing that and re-running the check.
All front-end vectors now match: 256 of 256, bit-exact. Next: the verification level for each design, and power at one decision per second.
Verification and measurement are done. Writing designs.md and report.md now.
The three designs are in `designs.md`. None has been trained: no EEG recordings came with the brief and this machine has no ML libraries, so there are no sensitivity or false-alarm numbers. I built each design with random placeholder weights to measure its size; the chip lab compiled all three and proved each circuit computes exactly its model.

| Design | Inputs | Layers | Parameters | Gates (optimised) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A: feature network** | 8 numbers summarising the last 2 s, 4 per channel: line length (how busy the signal is), amplitude, zero crossings, and line length above the patient's own background | 8 → 8 → 1, 4-bit weights | 81 | 2,367 |
| **B: time-pattern network** | line length every 0.25 s over the last 4 s, both channels | a small convolution over time (4 filters), keep each filter's peak, then 4 → 1 | 41 | 2,607 |
| **C: weights limited to −1, 0, +1** | power in 4 frequency bands plus line length, per channel | 10 → 16 → 1, no multipliers | 193 | 1,279 |

- **Line-length front-end:** the part that computes line length from the raw signal takes 396 gates.
- **Power:** at one decision per second, every classifier draws under 0.1 µW.
- **What these counts leave out:** the memory registers and the rest of each design's front-end. My unmeasured estimate is that C's frequency-band filters are the costliest, which may reverse the ranking.

**Second opinion:** I asked the cheap model (gpt-5-nano) for one feature to add. It suggested line length. I agree: it is a standard seizure feature and cheap in gates. Two caveats: it grows with signal strength, which varies between patients, so A measures it against the patient's own background. Chewing and movement also raise it, so the device only alarms after 3 positive seconds in a row.

**How to compare them:**
- **Data:** train on the CHB-MIT EEG set and test on the Siena EEG set, splitting by patient.
- **Metric:** seizures caught, false alarms per day, the worst single patient's detection rate, and time to alarm.
- **Circuit size:** gates for the whole chip, front-end included, not just the network.
- **Choice:** pick the smallest design that catches at least 90% of seizures with at most one false alarm a day.

`report.md` covers what was measured, what could not be done and the next step. The dashboard marks the reference-model and training stages as skipped.

Files are in the working folder:
- designs.md
- report.md
- spec.md
- designs/make_ir.py
